text.what: Hokkaido and Sakhalin: a woman's mouth ringed with indigo, begun in childhood and widened until she was ready to marry.
text.story:
The Ainu word *anchi-piri* carries the tool inside it — obsidian, and a cut. Ink came from the indigo plant. The mark was made by women on women, on the mouth, the forearms and the backs of the hands, and it grew with its owner: a small mark at five to thirteen, widened over years, finished when she married.

The Japanese state prohibited it. What happened next is the same everywhere on this site: the practice stops, the women who have it grow old, and the only pictures left are the ones outsiders took.

text.what: The Philippine traditions, tapped with a hafted thorn at ninety to a hundred and twenty strikes a minute.
text.story:
The Spanish called the Visayans *Pintados*, the painted ones, and recorded the tattoo as dress: a naked man "appears to be dressed in a kind of handsome armor engraved with very fine work" — worn at home with nothing but a loincloth, because the marks were the clothes.

The method is Austronesian and it is not poking. A needle — thorn, bone, horn, bamboo — is set perpendicular to a wooden handle in an L, and a second stick taps the handle. The hand that holds the tool never pushes; it positions. Ink is soot or ash in water, oil, cane juice or pig bile, and the design is laid out first in ink with a blade of grass or a length of string.

Among Cordilleran peoples tattoos were a form of clothing in the same explicit sense: to have none was to be naked. Chest work was not applied to a man until he had taken a head — which is why copying those designs today is held to be a bad idea, and why the men who fought in the 1960s and 70s were advised by elders not to take them.
text.today: Whang-od is ninety-something and tattooing in Buscalan; her apprentices are women, which breaks the inheritance rule her own community ran on, and her community accepted it. Around her there is a revival with a problem inside it: which designs are open.

names.name: Chin facial tattooing

when.label: Banned in the 1960s; the last tattooed women are elderly

practice.first_record_note: the Gazetteer of Upper Burma notices it in passing, and with contempt
practice.suppressed_by: banned in the 1960s by Burma's Union Revolutionary Council; discouraged by Christian and Buddhist missionaries
practice.note: Girls of fifteen to twenty. The design says which tribe, not which family.

text.what: Women's faces, marked between fifteen and twenty, in a pattern that names the tribe: full-face, part-face, dots, lines, or both.
text.story:
The designs differ by group and the differences are the point. M'kaan, Daai and Yin Du women are tattooed across the whole face; N'men and Matu women on certain parts of it; the Uppriu cover the face in dots; Ngagah mix vertical lines with dots; Daai set dots among vertical and horizontal lines on forehead and cheeks. Mro women wear small marks or stars on cheek, forehead or breast and tie them to fertility.

The explanation attached to the custom in almost every outside source is abduction: that a king took a beautiful Chin woman, that she disguised herself to get home, and that families marked their daughters so that no one would carry them off. The nineteenth-century British gazetteer repeats the abduction story and then adds that the anxiety "seems hardly justified by any beauty in the women themselves."

*Inference —* that sentence is worth leaving in. It is the clearest single demonstration on this site of what the colonial record is: the only written source for a great deal of this, and written by men who held the people they were describing in contempt. Read the fact, discount the frame.
text.today: Banned in the 1960s and discouraged by missionaries before that, the practice ended inside one generation. The women who carry it are elderly, and they are photographed constantly by visitors to the Chin hills. Whether that is documentation or a trade in faces is not a question this site settles.
text.notes: Northern and southern Chin groups differ; this record does not flatten sixty sub-groups into one design.

kin.as: The other Burmese tradition, and the one that was not banned.

text.story:
The Razzouk family carries the trade from Egypt to Jerusalem and still holds the carved olive-wood blocks that print the designs onto the skin before the needle follows. Coptic Christians in Egypt wear the wrist cross as an everyday identification, not only as a souvenir of a journey.

*Inference —* the wooden design blocks are the same idea as the Borneo stamp and the Burmese sample book: a hand tradition that needs a repertoire invents a way to store it outside a person's memory.

text.story:
*Godna* is the verb *to prick*, which puts it in the same family as *sak*, *kaki-*, and *deq*: the word for the tattoo is the word for what the needle does. The designs go on arms, hands, legs and face, and the practice runs through Baiga, Oraon, Birhor, Munda, Santal and many other communities, each with its own repertoire.

It travelled. The tattoo went with indentured workers to Guyana and Trinidad, which makes it one of very few traditions on this site with a diaspora that kept the marks.

text.story:
*Hajichi* went on the hands, where nothing conceals them, and it recorded a woman's passage — first marks in girlhood, more at betrothal, the set completed at marriage. Japan prohibited it in 1899 while assimilating the Ryukyu kingdom, and enforcement was real enough that the practice went underground and then out.

*Inference —* the ban's design is worth noticing. A mark on the hands cannot be covered by clothing, which makes it the easiest tattoo in the world to police and the hardest to keep quietly.
text.notes: Okinawan women, in Okinawa and in the diaspora, have been taking hajichi up again; this site has no count of how many.

practice.first_record_note: the fullest description this site can name is Shway Yoe's, 1882; the custom is far older

practice.sessions: three to six days for the whole; three or four figures at a sitting

text.what: Every up-country Burmese man wore one: a sheet of dark-blue animals from the navel to below the knee, begun in boyhood.
text.story:
Shway Yoe — the pen name of Sir James George Scott, who lived in Burma and wrote the fullest account of it in English — opens the chapter flatly: a Burmese youth counts his thigh tattooing as important as his entry into a monastery, and until it is done "there may be doubts as to his thorough manhood."

The finished work runs from a line level with the navel to just past the kneecap, and he reaches for a garment to describe it: not a marking of the skin so much as **"a skin-tight pair of caleçons, fitting better than the best glove ever made."** The figures are tigers, cats, monkeys, elephants, *nats* and *bilus* — each one framed in an oval of letters, each frame its own setting, the gaps filled with the same tracery.

The frame is the tell. The animals are not a scene; they are a repeating field of self-contained units, which is why the whole reads at a distance as cloth rather than as a picture.

*Attested —* a good *saya* carried a sample book of drawings so the boy could pick his patterns and their places before the opium went in. A tattoo studio's flash sheet, in Burma, in 1882.
text.today: Lethwei fighters — Burmese bareknuckle boxers — carry the leg work as the sport's own mark, and the Wikipedia article on tattooing in Myanmar records fighters describing the sitting, up to 24 hours across both legs, as the thing to be endured without showing it. Outside the ring it is a thinning tradition rather than a general one.
text.notes: Shway Yoe reports and then refuses a claim: that the custom began for a "shameful reason assigned by foreign writers." He does not repeat the reason and says no Burman believes it. This site does the same.

names.said: A journey mark, a headhunter's hands, an aubergine flower on each shoulder

text.what: Borneo: tapped designs carved on a block and printed onto the skin, with hand marks reserved for a man who had taken a head.
text.story:
The Iban mark a journey. *Bungai terung*, the aubergine flower, goes on each shoulder when a young man leaves on *bejalai* — the walkabout that makes him an adult. The *entegulun*, the hand tattoo, is not a decoration: it records that the wearer took a head. Anthony Bourdain filmed one of the last men entitled to it.

The design source is the striking part. Borneo tattooists carved patterns onto wooden blocks, inked the block, printed it onto the skin, and then tapped along the printed line — a stamp, a stencil and a tool in one, and a way of keeping a repertoire that does not depend on memory.
text.notes: Hose and McDougall, 1912, are the fullest colonial description and carry the usual freight; the Iban record their own designs now.

text.what: Japan: needles bound with silk to a wooden rod, worked by hand — *tebori*, carving by hand — over years, in a design that covers the body like a garment.
text.story:
The word says the method: *irezumi*, inserting ink. Nara ink goes grey-blue under the skin. A full back piece is not a session but a relationship, and the shape it takes — shoulders, chest panels, a gap down the sternum — is a suit of clothes that can be closed over.

The Meiji government outlawed it while courting foreign opinion, and foreigners promptly came to Japan to be tattooed. The occupation legalised it in 1948. Japanese law then held for decades that tattooing needed a medical licence, until a 2020 decision ended that. The criminal association it acquired under the ban has outlived the ban by seventy years.

text.what: Inuit tattoos: women's work on women's skin, stitched with a sooted thread drawn under the skin, or poked.
text.story:
The method is the rarest on this site. A needle carries a sinew thread blackened with soot and is drawn *through* the skin, leaving the pigment behind it in a line — sewing, with the line left in. The same hands did the sewing that kept people alive in a cold place.

The marks answered to Sedna, whose severed fingers became the sea animals: hand and arm tattoos refer to where her hands were cut. A woman without hand marks was refused the good afterlife; a woman without face marks went to the land of the crestfallen, where the smoke rises from her throat and her head hangs down.

Then missionaries, the schools, and a century of silence. The revival is recent, documented and deliberate: Hovak Johnston's project began putting traditional marks back on Inuit women in 2016, learning the stitch from the elders who still remembered it.

text.what: The Lanna leg tattoo: waist to knee, sometimes to the ankle, dense enough that the murals paint it as a pair of black trousers.
text.story:
A Lanna volume held in the wichaa.net manuscript corpus puts it plainly: temple murals show northern Thai men tattooed *จนดูเหมือนนุ่งกางเกงสีดำ* — "until it looked as if they wore black trousers." Elders quoted in the same passage give the extent: the legs in patterns from the waist down to the ankles, the torso front and back, the arms, even the fingers; some as far as the neck and the crown of the head.

The enforcement was talk. A man who did not tattoo his legs and torso "would be gossiped about as being like a woman — lacking the endurance to bear the needle"; if he had no marks he might as well put on a *sin*, the woman's wrapped skirt. The work went to a master in the community and the fee had a Lanna name of its own, **khan tang** (ขันตั้ง), where central Thai says *khan khru*.

*Inference —* the tradition is described here in the past tense by its own inheritors, not by an outside authority, and nothing in the passage names a law. What it names is electric light: the old night courtship ended, the reason a young man needed to be looked at ended with it, and the marks went out of use within about a generation.
text.today: Sak kha lai is not what a visitor to Chiang Mai is offered. What is offered is **sak yant** — the same needle, a different job. The leg tattoo covered a man; the yant marks him with a formula.
text.notes: This site treats sak kha lai and sak yant as two traditions on one hand, not one tradition with two names. That separation is the client's correction, and it is the same separation the Burmese record makes between the thigh work and the charms.

practice.note: A formula in letters and figures, laid on the skin, held by rules the bearer keeps afterwards.

text.what: Letters, numbers and figures arranged into a diagram — *yant* — and pricked into skin with a long needle.
text.story:
*Sak* is the verb: to prick. The Khmer root *cɔkʔ* means the same, and the Khmer dictionary keeps the word native rather than borrowed from Sanskrit. *Yant* is the diagram — the same word as Sanskrit *yantra*, the same family as the yantra drawn on cloth, on brass, on paper.

The Lanna volume explains why it moved to skin at all, and the reason is logistics: a yant on paper or metal is left at home. A yant on the body is carried. Everything else — which formula, which animal, which direction the letters run — follows from that one decision.

Two corrections this site carries, both from the client and both checkable. **Most sak yant is not done at Wat Bang Phra.** That temple is what the film crews know; the ordinary route is an ajarn or a monk near where you live. And **Khom is not "what a yant is written in."** Khom script is the central Thai convention. In the north the letters are northern Thai — *tua mueang*, the Tai Tham script — or Shan, or Tai Lue.
text.today: Chiang Mai has working masters, and one operation there publishes the lineage of every one of them — who taught whom, which temple, how many years in the robe and how many out. That published lineage is the closest thing this site has to a family tree for a living hand tradition.
text.notes: The designs themselves are indexed on wichaa.net at /yant: 36 named designs across 63 plates, entered by what each one is for.

text.what: The same leg work as the Burmese, carried further — to the ankles, up the back, and on the specialists who tattooed everybody else's charms.
text.story:
Leslie Milne lived among the northern Shan and published *Shans at Home* in 1910. Her sentence on status is the whole of it: **a Shan boy is a child until he is tattooed.** Plucky boys start at twelve, most wait until fourteen. The rule is both legs, waist to knee, the thighs completely covered in dark blue — and often on to the ankles. Backs come later, in blue or more often red, and without symmetry: a grid of lettered squares under one shoulder blade, small circles or beasts on the other side.

Shway Yoe, writing thirty years earlier, says the Shans tattoo more extensively than the Burmese, with rays running up from the waistline to the chest and nearly to the nape, and that the retainers of a *sawbwa* — a Shan chief — might be marked everywhere but the palms and the soles.

The second thing he says is the one that matters for the whole region: **the men who tattoo charms and cabalistic figures are mostly Shans.** They are credited with the special skill, they mutter the spells over the medicine, and they are held in some awe for it. The Lanna volume agrees from the other side of the border: this fashion was widespread among the Burmese and the Tai Yai, who tattoo yantras no less than the Lanna do.
text.today: Tai Yai communities span the Myanmar–Thailand border, including Mae Hong Son. This site has no count of who is still tattooed and does not guess at one.

text.story:
Two nineteenth-century observers recorded it — the archaeologist Ćiro Truhelka, who drew the designs, and a doctor, Leopold Glück, who published a paper in Vienna in 1894 titled *The Tattooing of Skin Among the Catholics of Bosnia and Herzegovina*.

The custom went out after the Second World War. What survives is the design vocabulary, now being applied by machine by tattooists in Croatia and Bosnia — a revival of the pattern without the practice, which is a distinct thing and this site counts it separately.

text.story:
Two lineages meet here and they are not the same thing. One is improvised: a sewing needle or a safety pin, ballpoint ink, done by a friend, associated with prisons and with people too young to be tattooed legally. The other is professional hand-poke, done with medical needles in a studio, which is now a standing style with its own practitioners.

*Inference —* this site lists it as a tradition because it is one, and because the same word covers both ends of it. The difference between the two is not the method; it is whether the needle is sterile and whether the person holding it has been taught.

text.what: New Zealand: albatross-bone chisels struck with a mallet, cutting a groove that stays visible as texture, not only as colour.
text.story:
*Tā moko* is not a puncture. The *uhi* — a hafted chisel of albatross bone — is struck, and the skin keeps the furrow. That is why a moko reads in raking light and why a photograph flattens it.

Pigment: *awheto*, a caterpillar fungus, for the body; *ngarehu*, burnt timber, for the darker face colour; soot from burnt kauri gum mixed with fat. It was kept in carved vessels called *oko* which were buried between uses and handed down.

Steel needles arrived with Europeans and were faster and safer, and the groove went. Men's moko had largely stopped by the 1860s; women kept receiving *moko kauae* into the twentieth century, and Michael King interviewed more than seventy women in the early 1970s who had been marked before the Tohunga Suppression Act of 1907. Since 1990 the practice has come back, machine mostly, chisel too, with women among the practitioners — and a Māori foreign minister and a prime-time news anchor wearing *moko kauae* on the country's screens.

text.what: Samoa: a comb of bone and turtle shell, struck with a mallet, covering a man from the middle of the back to the knees.
text.story:
The English word *tattoo* comes from this word. The *tufuga tā tatau* works with two assistants, the *'au toso*, who stretch the skin and wipe; the titles are hereditary in two families, the Sa Su'a of Savai'i and the Sa Tulou'ena of Upolu, and Samoan masters tattooed Tongan and Fijian chiefly families too.

The clothing logic is explicit here as well: an untattooed Samoan man is *telefua* or *telenoa* — naked. A man who starts the *pe'a* and cannot finish carries *pe'a mutu*, an unfinished tattoo, and that is a mark of shame that the finished work is designed to prevent.

Samoa credits Fiji with the origin, in a song about twin sisters who swam across with a basket of tools, singing that only women should be tattooed — and arrived singing the opposite.

text.story:
By 1908 there was one recorded practitioner left — a woman called Rabali, tattooing until about 1910. That is as close as this site gets to a date for the end of a tradition, and it comes with a name.

The revival is as precisely dated. The Veiqia Project, a collective of Fijian women artists, took the practice up from the archives and the objects in the 2010s. Samoa's own origin story sends the tatau across from Fiji, which makes the revived practice older than the one that borrowed it.

text.what: The skin is cut or chiselled and pigment is rubbed into the cut, so the mark has a texture as well as a colour.
text.story:
Māori *tā moko* is the clearest case: the *uhi*, a hafted chisel of albatross bone, is struck with a mallet and the skin keeps a groove. A moko made this way catches light. A moko made with a needle does not, which is exactly what changed when steel arrived — and why some practitioners have taken the chisel up again.

The Ainu word *anchi-piri* names obsidian and a cut. Among the Lumad and Negrito peoples of the Philippines a hafted chisel incises the skin in short dashes, and the result is partly scarification.
text.notes: Cutting shades into scarification, which is a different practice with a different point. The test used here: if pigment is put into the wound to be seen afterwards, it is on this site.

when.label: Samuel O'Reilly's patent, and everything after it

text.what: An electric motor drives the needle, at speeds between fifty and three thousand insertions a minute. It is here for contrast.
text.story:
Until 1891 there was no need for the phrase *hand-poked*. Every tattoo in every tradition on this site was made by hand, and the differences that mattered were between a comb and a point, a chisel and a needle.

*Inference —* the machine did not only speed the work up; it renamed everything else. "Traditional", "hand", "by hand" are all retroactive labels, applied after a machine existed to distinguish them from. That is worth holding on to when a tradition is described as having "resisted" the machine: most of them had no opinion about a device that did not exist when the practice was formed.

names.name: Poke
names.said: One point, pushed in by the hand that holds it

text.what: A point held in the hand and pushed into the skin, once per mark, with the pigment carried on or into the hole.
text.story:
The hand does the work: it provides the force, the depth and the rhythm. A poked line is a row of punctures close enough to read as continuous — Shway Yoe's description of the Burmese method is exactly that, "a series of punctures close together, forming what afterwards fades into a rough line."

The tool can be a thorn, a fish bone, a sewing needle, a sharpened bamboo splint or a two-foot weighted brass rod. What makes it poking is that nothing strikes the tool and nothing drives it but the hand.
text.how: Depth is the whole skill. Too shallow and the mark leaves with the skin; too deep and the pigment spreads under it and the line thickens with age.

text.story:
Skin stitching is the Arctic method, and it belongs to the same set of hands and the same needle case as the sewing that made the clothing people survived in. Nothing is punctured repeatedly; the line goes in once.

It is the rarest method on this site — two traditions out of the whole map — and the one that most clearly cannot be done by machine.

names.name: Tap
names.said: A comb set crosswise on a handle, struck by a second stick

text.what: A needle or a comb of needles fixed at a right angle to a handle, and a second piece of wood striking the handle to drive it in.
text.story:
This is the Austronesian method, and it runs from Taiwan through the Philippines and Borneo across the whole Pacific: Samoa, Tonga, Fiji, the Marquesas, Hawaii. The rate is about 90 to 120 taps a minute, which is a drum tempo, and the sound is what a tattooing session sounds like in half the traditions on this site.

*Inference —* the hand that holds the comb does not push. It positions and holds the angle; the striking hand supplies the force. That division of labour is what lets a wide comb lay down a band of solid black at a speed no single point can match, and it is why the Pacific traditions cover so much more skin than the poking ones.
text.notes: This site keeps tapping separate from poking rather than folding both into "hand-poked". They are different tools, different rates and different results, and the traditions that use them know the difference.

text.what: Not a needle: a carved wooden block, inked and printed onto the skin, so the tattooist follows a line instead of remembering one.
text.story:
Three traditions on this site solved the same problem the same way and had no contact with each other. Borneo tattooists carved designs into wooden blocks, printed them onto the skin and tapped along the print. The Razzouk family in Jerusalem still holds olive-wood blocks three hundred years old and still prints pilgrims' crosses from them. And Shway Yoe reports that a good Burmese *saya* carried **a sample book of drawings** so the boy could choose his figures and their positions before the opium went in.

*Inference —* a flash sheet, a stencil and a catalogue are all the same invention, and it arrives wherever a hand tradition has more designs than one person can hold.

text.what: A brass rod about two feet long, weighted at the top with a cast figure, with a split four-way point at the other end.
text.story:
Shway Yoe describes it part by part in 1882 and the design is a solved problem. The *yat*, the style, is solid with a round sharp point, split into four by long slits at right angles — the slits hold the pigment, so the tool carries its own ink. The style is about four inches and fits into a hollow pipe, which joins it to the weighted end. **The weight is at the top and the length is hollow**, so the tool has mass where mass helps and none where it would tire the hand.

The weight is cast as a bird, a *nat* or a *bilu*, and a good *saya*'s is carved elaborately. The tattooist catches the shaft in his right hand and rests the point in a fork made by the left forefinger and thumb, the left hand flat on the body — the hand becomes the guide rail.
text.how: Ink is lampblack from burnt sesame oil, mixed with water as it is wanted. The outline goes on first with a camel-hair brush.

text.what: The sak yant needle: a long steel or brass shaft, pushed with one hand and steered with the other.
text.story:
The grip is the same one Shway Yoe drew in Burma and the same one a visitor photographs in Chiang Mai today — the driving hand, the guiding fork of finger and thumb, the skin pulled tight by an assistant or by the bearer's own posture. A single design takes a sitting.

The modern working needle is steel, single-use, and that is the part of the practice that has changed most in fifty years.

instrument.length_note: a working length of roughly 40–60 cm is usual; this site has measured none
instrument.points: a single point, or a point split to hold ink

text.what: The northern instrument: an iron stylus of the kind used to incise palm-leaf manuscripts, taken to skin.
text.story:
The word *char* (จาร) is the verb for writing on a palm leaf with a stylus — scoring the surface and rubbing soot into the score so the letters appear. The same word, the same tool family, and in the north the same people: the men who could write the letters were the men who could put them on a body.

*Inference —* that overlap explains something about the region's tattooing that a picture of a tiger does not. A Lanna yant is a written document. The tool is a pen, the surface is a person, and the fee has the same name as a teacher's fee because the transaction is a teaching one.
text.notes: Ten pages of the manuscript corpus this site counted carry the word เหล็กจาร. None of them is a tattooing manual; they are about writing.

text.story:

text.story:
Pigment lived in carved vessels called *oko*, buried between uses and passed down the generations. A feeding funnel, the *kōrere*, was used while a face was healing.

Steel needles replaced the *uhi* in the late nineteenth century: faster, safer, and smooth. In 2007 it was reported back in use by some practitioners.

names.name: Lampblack
names.th: เขม่าตะเกียง
names.said: Soot off a burning oil lamp, the best from sesame oil

text.what: Soot collected from a lamp, mixed with water as it is needed. Under the skin it reads blue-black, and it does not leave.
text.story:
Shway Yoe names the grade: the best lampblack is the soot of burning sesame oil. The Burmese black recipe recorded on the Myanmar article is more elaborate — soot mixed with dried gallbladder of fish or cattle, powdered, boiled, simmered with bitter melon leaves and dried to a paste until wanted.

The two colours behaved differently and everyone noticed. Milne, on the Shan: tattooing in red sometimes fades, the blue appears to be indelible. Shway Yoe, on the Burmese: the blue dye from the lampblack never disappears, the vermilion gradually fades away.

*Inference —* that difference decided what each colour was used for. Identity, manhood and the leg work went in black, for life. Charms went in red, and a charm that fades is a charm that can be renewed — which is a feature, not a fault.

text.what: Soot mixed with breast milk, reported as the Kurdish preparation.
text.story: *Inference —* the additive in every one of these recipes is something sticky and mildly antiseptic that the household already has: milk, honey, bile, fat, oil. The carbon does the marking; the liquid decides how it handles.

names.name: Soot and water
names.said: The commonest ink on earth: something burnt, something wet

text.what: Ash or soot from a fire, ground and mixed with water, oil, plant juice or animal bile.
text.story:
Across the whole map the base ingredient is carbon and the variable is the liquid. The Philippines: soot or ashes with water, oil, plant extracts like sugarcane juice, or pig bile. Kurdistan: soot with breast milk, reportedly. Bosnia: soot with honey, and sometimes saliva. Ötzi's marks were made from soot or fireplace ash.

*Inference —* carbon is the pigment every human group already had. Any fire makes it, it does not fade, and the particle is large enough to stay where it is put. Nothing else available before industrial chemistry does all three.

names.said: Red mercury sulphide, for charms, and it fades

text.what: Cinnabar red, diluted, mixed with herbs and other things, and used for charms rather than for the standing marks.
text.story:
Shway Yoe: all the more important charms are reserved for other parts of the body and executed in vermilion. The *a-nu se*, the drug of tenderness, is vermilion mixed with herbs and the dried skin of the *tokay* gecko; a few dots in a triangle between the eyes are enough.

It fades — everybody says so — and a fading charm gets redone.

*Attested —* the mercury in cinnabar is toxic. The sources this site quotes do not raise that, and it is not offered here as advice about anything; it is a fact about the pigment named in them.

text.story:
Shway Yoe: each representation is surrounded by a roughly oval tracery of letters, which forms a curious and remarkably effective frame, so each animal has a setting of its own — and vacant spaces are filled the same way, the top and bottom finished with a scalloped line.

Sometimes the letters are said to carry a cabalistic meaning; ordinarily, he says, no more is claimed for them than beauty. The serious charms go elsewhere on the body, usually in vermilion.

*Inference —* the frame is what makes the leg read as cloth. A repeating field of bounded units is a textile pattern; a scene is a picture. These traditions chose the textile.

names.name: Khan tang
names.said: The teacher's bowl — the Lanna word, where the centre says khan khru

text.what: The fee, set by the master, presented in a bowl: flowers, candles, incense, cloth, coins, and whatever else that master's line asks for.
text.story:
The Lanna volume gives the word and the mechanism in one line: the man goes to a community master expert in yant tattooing, and there is a teacher's fee, *khan tang*, as the master sets it.

*Khan* is the pedestalled bowl. *Tang* is to set up. The same word covers the offering that opens a course of study in any Lanna craft — which is the tell: **the transaction is not a purchase, it is an enrolment.** Central Thai calls the same thing *khan khru*.

A price list is a different object and it exists too; a Chiang Mai operation publishes one. This site keeps the two apart rather than translating one into the other.

*ขัน* คือภาชนะมีเชิง *ตั้ง* คือจัดขึ้น คำเดียวกันนี้ใช้กับการขึ้นครูของงานช่างล้านนาทุกแขนง ซึ่งเป็นจุดสังเกต **นี่ไม่ใช่การซื้อ แต่เป็นการขึ้นครู** ภาคกลางเรียกสิ่งเดียวกันว่าขันครู

names.said: What the bearer keeps afterwards, or the mark stops working

text.what: A yant works while its bearer keeps the rules that came with it — most often a list of foods not eaten and things not done.
text.story:
The condition is the structure. A tattoo that has to be maintained by conduct is a contract with a term, and it explains why these traditions can be strict about who receives what: the mark is the easy part and the keeping is the rest of it.

The same logic runs through the Burmese charms, which are renewed when they fade, and through the Fijian and Samoan fee, which is paid before the work rather than after.

names.name: Bearing it
names.said: Opium in Burma, friends shouting advice among the Shan, a straight face in the ring

text.what: In tradition after tradition the pain is not a side effect of the mark. It is the thing being demonstrated.
text.story:
Burma: the boy is put under opium, and some parents refuse it, and a few boys have died of the dose. Three or four figures at a sitting. The Shan: the friends sit round in a circle telling him not to scratch, that he is wriggling too much, that no girl will admire a spoiled pattern. Lethwei fighters: up to twenty-four hours across both legs, and the point is the straight face.

Samoa: a man who starts the *pe'a* and cannot finish wears *pe'a mutu*, an unfinished tattoo, and it is a mark of shame. Lanna: a man who will not bear the needle should put on a woman's skirt.

*Inference —* every tradition that uses the mark to certify endurance also needs the mark to be visible and hard to fake. That is the same reason the work is put where it cannot be hidden and takes long enough to be witnessed.
text.notes: Anaesthetic, where it was used at all, was opium. No source here describes the modern options, and this site gives no advice about any of it.

text.what: The date is rarely free. Most traditions on this site fix the work to a passage the person is making anyway.
text.story:
Bamar: the waist tattoo is done before or soon after temporary ordination as a monk — two rites of passage stacked on one season. Shan: twelve for the bold, fourteen for most. Chin: fifteen to twenty. Ainu: from five to thirteen, widened until marriage. Kalinga and Cordilleran: after the act that earns it. Atayal: a man's chin after he fathers a child.

*Inference —* a mark made at a moment is a dated document. It is how these traditions record a life without writing anything down.

text.what: Nobody is tattooed alone. The room is part of the method.
text.story:
Samoa: the *'au toso*, two assistants, stretch the skin and wipe. Fiji: one older woman applies the marks and others hold the young woman still. Burma: the tattooist's own left hand is the rest for the tool, flat against the body. Shan: the friends sit in a circle for days afterwards, because the itching is worse than the work.

*Inference —* the skin has to be tight or the point wanders, which makes at least one extra pair of hands a technical requirement rather than a social one. The witnesses come free with it.

text.what: Two of the Chiang Mai masters whose published profiles give a teacher, a temple, and a count of years in and out of the robe.
text.story:
Ajarn Dang: thirty-three years of practice, ten of them as a monk, a fifth-generation family line, trained under Sukhawaphuthargo. Ajarn Sak: eighteen years, twelve as a monk, a line through his father and grandfather, Burmese magic and the northern Tai Yai forest tradition.

That second line matters for this site's argument. A working Chiang Mai master describes his own training as Burmese and Tai Yai — which is the same border-crossing Shway Yoe described from the other side in 1882, when he wrote that the men who tattooed charms were mostly Shans.
text.notes: Both tattooed this site's publisher. The pictures here that come from those sessions are used with permission and credited as such.

text.story:
Shway Yoe: "I have had fifteen figures done in little over half an hour. But then Saya Chein is a celebrated man."

names.said: A colonial officer writing under a Burmese pen name

when.label: The Burman: His Life and Notions, 1882

text.what: The Scottish administrator who wrote the fullest English description of Burmese tattooing, under a Burmese pen name, in 1882.
text.story:
James George Scott went to Burma as a journalist, stayed as an administrator, and published *The Burman: His Life and Notions* as "Shway Yoe" — a Burmese name, on a book about Burmese life, by a man who then spent decades extending British rule over the Shan States and compiling the *Gazetteer of Upper Burma* that this site also quotes.

The chapter on tattooing is the best single source on the *htoe kwin* in English. It is also written by the administration. Both of those are true at once, and this site cites the detail while naming the hand.

*Inference —* the pen name is the thing to keep in view. A book that speaks as a Burman, written by the officer annexing the Shan States, is the whole problem of the colonial record in one byline.

names.name: Truhelka and Glück
names.said: An archaeologist who drew it and a doctor who published it, 1894

when.label: Vienna, 1894

text.what: The two men who recorded Bosnian sicanje in the 1890s: Ćiro Truhelka, who illustrated the designs, and Leopold Glück, who published the paper.
text.story:
Glück's title says exactly what it is: *Die Tätowirung der Haut bei den Katholiken Bosniens und der Herzegowina*, Vienna, 1894. A doctor and an archaeologist, writing for an Austro-Hungarian readership about the people their empire had just occupied.

*Inference —* that pairing recurs across this whole site. The professions that produced the record are medicine, administration and archaeology, which is why so much of it reads as measurement of a body rather than description of a practice.

names.name: Whang-od Oggay
names.said: Mambabatok, Buscalan

when.label: Tattooing since about fifteen

text.what: The Kalinga *mambabatok* everyone has heard of, tapping in Buscalan since she was about fifteen.
text.story:
She learned from her father, and that was already an exception: only men with tattooing ancestry were supposed to learn. Her own apprentices are women, which is a second exception, and her community accepted it.

She tattooed headhunters who had earned the marks. She never married and has no children, and under the inheritance rule that would end the line — which is why the apprentices matter and why she chose them the way she did.
text.notes: Buscalan now receives a stream of visitors who come to be tattooed by her. Whether that is a living tradition or a queue is argued about by people who live there, and this site does not adjudicate it.

*Inference —* a mural is evidence that a painter expected to see marked legs, which is not quite the same as evidence of any particular man's marks. It is strong for pattern and weak for detail, and this site treats it that way.

names.name: Where the marks go
names.said: Counted across every tradition on the site

text.what: Each tradition here records which zones of the body it marks. Counted together, the zones sort into two kinds.
text.story:
**Zones that can be covered** — thighs, back, chest, waist-to-knee — belong to traditions where the tattoo is a garment and the wearer chooses when it is seen. **Zones that cannot** — face, chin, hands, fingers — belong to traditions where the mark is an identification, and where a state that wanted the practice stopped could enforce the ban by looking at people.

*Inference —* the second group is where the bans land. Chin faces, Atayal faces, Okinawan hands, Ainu mouths, Māori chins. The leg traditions were not banned; they faded. **A mark you cannot hide is easy to police, and a mark under a longyi is not worth the trouble.**
text.notes: Counted from the `placement` field on every tradition record; the chart prints how many records carried the field.

names.name: The tattoo is clothing
names.said: Three languages, three centuries, three continents, one metaphor

text.what: Sources in Burmese, Northern Thai, Spanish and Samoan — and a Cordilleran rule recorded in English — reach for the same comparison: the tattoo is not on the body, it is what the body wears.
text.story:
Shway Yoe, Burma, 1882, on the finished *htoe kwin*: the effect is "not so much of a marking of the cuticle as of **a skin-tight pair of caleçons**, fitting better than the best glove ever made."

A Lanna volume, northern Thailand, describing the same region's work from its own side: men tattooed their bodies **จนดูเหมือนนุ่งกางเกงสีดำ** — "until it looked as if they wore black trousers" — and a man with no marks should put on a woman's skirt instead.

A Spanish account of the Visayans: a naked tattooed man "appears to be **dressed in a kind of handsome armor** engraved with very fine work… their dress at home and in their barrio is their tattoos and a *bahag*."

The Cordillerans: having no tattoos was **equated to being naked**. The Samoans: an untattooed man is **telefua** or **telenoa** — naked, in the ordinary word, not as a figure of speech.

*Inference —* this is the one comparison that survives translation everywhere on this map, and it is doing work. A garment is the thing that makes a person presentable in public; it is put on at a particular age; its absence is shameful rather than merely unusual; and it is the first thing another person reads. Every one of those is also true of the marks. **Where a tradition covers a whole zone of the body, its own sources describe that zone as dressed.**
text.notes: The count of traditions on this site whose sources use the clothing comparison is computed at build time and printed on the page rather than asserted here.

names.name: The leg-tattoo zone
names.said: Burma, the Shan States and Lanna — and the border is not the border

text.what: One custom, four peoples, and a boundary that runs through the middle of modern Thailand rather than along its edge.
text.story:
Put the sources side by side.

**Burma, 1882.** Shway Yoe: every up-country man is tattooed from the navel to below the kneecap. Not a single *taw-tha*, the sturdy man of the small towns and villages, is without it.

**The Shan States, 1910.** Milne: a Shan boy is a child until he is tattooed; the rule is both legs, waist to knee, and often on to the ankles. Shway Yoe adds that the Shans go further than the Burmese — up the back, to the nape, and among a chief's retainers, everywhere but palms and soles.

**Lanna.** The Lanna volume: men tattooed until it looked as if they wore black trousers, waist to ankle, torso, arms, fingers — and "this fashion was widespread among the Burmese and the Tai Yai, who tattoo yantras no less than the Lanna."

**Siam.** Milne, in the same paragraph where she says the Shans learned it from the Burmese: "the Siamese, who are so closely related to them, **tattoo themselves very slightly, or not at all**."

*Inference —* that last line is usually read as a fact about Thailand. It is a fact about **central** Thailand. Milne was comparing the Shan to Bangkok, and Lanna — which was a tributary kingdom, not a province, until 1899 — is on the other side of her comparison. The leg tattoo's territory is the Tai-Buddhist upland: Burma, the Shan States, the Tai Khuen and Tai Lue towns, and Lanna. **The edge of the zone runs through modern Thailand, roughly where Lanna ended, and the colonial record could not see it because it was reading the map by kingdoms.**

This is what the map on this page is drawing, and it is the one map on the site that no source draws for it.
text.notes: The zone is drawn from four written sources and one manuscript. It is not a survey, nobody counted tattooed men anywhere, and the outline is this project's reading rather than anyone's measurement.

when.label: Banned at the opening of Meiji; legalised under the occupation

text.what: Japan banned tattooing while presenting itself to the world, and foreigners immediately travelled there to be tattooed.
text.story:
The ban was about image. The practice continued underground, tattooists worked on visiting sailors and princes, and the association with criminality that the ban created outlasted the ban by three generations. Osaka's mayor was still surveying city employees about their tattoos in 2012, and the courts found against him.

The Ryukyus got their own prohibition in 1899, aimed at *hajichi* on women's hands. Taiwan's Atayal were banned from facial tattooing in 1930 by the same administration.

*Inference —* three bans, one state, sixty years, and each one targets the marks of a people being absorbed. The Meiji ban is usually told as a story about respectability. Seen with the other two, it is a story about who gets to look like themselves.

text.what: Spain called the Visayans *Pintados*, the painted ones, described their tattoos in detail, and converted them out of the practice within two centuries.
text.story:
The Spanish accounts are careful and admiring. They describe the tattoo as clothing; they record that no tattooing was begun until a brave deed had been performed and that each further panel needed another; they note that men tattooed even their chins and around the eyes so that they appeared masked.

Then the same administration's church ended it. In the lowlands the tradition is gone and the description survives. In the Cordillera, where Spain never held the mountains, the practice survives and the Spanish description does not apply.

*Inference —* on this site that is the clearest natural experiment there is: one people, two zones, the same century, and the difference is entirely whether the coloniser could get there.

text.what: Several traditions here stopped and came back. Where both ends are datable, this site subtracts them and prints the gap.
text.story:
Fiji: one tattooist left by 1908; an artists' collective takes it up again in the 2010s. Inuit: missionaries and the schools; a revitalisation project from 2016. Māori: the 1907 Act; the resurgence from 1990. Okinawa: the 1899 prohibition; hands being marked again now.

The gaps run to roughly a century each. *Inference —* what carries a practice across a hundred years is not a book. In every case on this list the bridge is a person: the elders Hovak Johnston learned the stitch from, the seventy women Michael King interviewed in the 1970s, the museum objects the Veiqia Project worked from, and the grandmothers.

A practice with no living bearer left is a different problem, and the Lanna leg tattoo is in that category.

names.name: What the word means first
names.said: Prick, strike, write, pattern

text.what: The word each tradition uses for the tattoo, and what it meant before it meant that.
text.story:
Four families, and they line up with the method rather than with the geography.

**Prick** — Thai and Khmer *sak*, Inuktitut *kaki-*, Hindi *godna*, Kurdish *deq*, Croatian *sicanje*, Burmese *htoe*, Okinawan *hajichi*. Every one of them is a poking tradition, and the word is the verb for what the needle does.

**Strike** — Samoan and Polynesian *tatau*, Māori *tā*, Marquesan *patu*. Every one of them is a tapping tradition, and the word is the verb for the mallet.

**Pattern** — Austronesian *batok*, *patik*, *burik*; Northern Thai *lai*. The word is the design, and it is the same word used for the pattern on a pot or a cloth.

**Write** — Atayal *ptasan*; and in Lanna, the tool for tattooing is the same *lek char* stylus used to write a palm-leaf manuscript.

*Inference —* a language names the tattoo after whichever part of it that culture finds most salient: the movement, the tool, the design, or the literacy. Four answers, and none of them is "the picture".

names.said: 61 marks, mostly on the legs, about 3300 BCE

when.label: Radiocarbon range for the body

text.what: The Alpine body with sixty-one tattoos — nineteen groups of black lines, and the greatest concentration on the legs.
text.story:
The marks are 1–3 mm wide and 7–40 mm long: groups of parallel lines along the body's long axis and either side of the lumbar spine, a cross behind the right knee, another at the right ankle, parallel lines round the left wrist. Twelve of the nineteen groups are on the legs.

Microscopy on samples showed the pigment was made from fireplace soot.

*Inference —* the oldest tattooed body in Europe is a set of short lines on the legs and lower back, put there with soot. Five thousand years later, the *htoe kwin* is a leg tattoo made with lamp soot. Nothing connects them and the resemblance is not a lineage; it is what the available tools and the available pigment produce.

The Lanna volume rests its case on exactly this: the evidence for the custom is the murals in important temples, which show men tattooed until they look dressed.

*Inference —* a mural is good evidence for three things — that the custom existed, roughly what area of the body it covered, and that it was ordinary enough to paint without comment. It is weak evidence for the designs themselves: painters simplify, and a wall painted with a hundred figures is not a pattern book. This site reads the murals for extent and does not read them for detail.

names.name: What counts as hand-poked
names.said: Tapping is not poking, and both are hands

text.what: The site is called hand poke and half the traditions on it do not poke. Here is the line it draws and why the line is arguable.
text.story:
A poked tattoo is driven by the hand holding the tool. A tapped one is driven by a second stick striking a hafted comb. A stitched one is sewn. A cut one is chiselled or incised and then rubbed with pigment.

All four are hand methods and none of them is a machine, which is why they are all here. But calling them all "hand-poke" flattens the thing each tradition is proudest of, so this site keeps them as four and says which is which on every record.

The hard cases are real. Māori *uhi* work was replaced by needle work in the nineteenth century and the tradition kept its name. Modern professional hand-poke uses a cartridge needle in a stabiliser pen, which is a tool with a handle and a grip and no motor. **A reader who would draw the line somewhere else is looking at the same field on the same records and can re-sort it.**

names.name: Who wrote it down
names.said: An administrator, a doctor, a missionary, an archaeologist

text.what: Most of what is known about the stopped traditions was written by the people whose arrival stopped them.
text.story:
Shway Yoe was Sir James George Scott, who wrote as a Burman and spent his career extending British rule over the Shan States. Leopold Glück was a doctor in occupied Bosnia. Ćiro Truhelka was an archaeologist in the same administration. Hose and McDougall were a colonial officer and a psychologist. The Gazetteer of Upper Burma is a government publication, and in the middle of a paragraph about Chin women's faces it stops to insult them.

This site uses all of it, because there is nothing else, and it names the writer every time. **The detail is usually reliable and the frame usually is not** — a measurement of a tool, a rate of work, a fee, an age, a sequence, these are the things an observer can get right. Why people did it, what they believed, what it meant: on those, the source is guessing about people it does not respect.

The Lanna volume in the corpus is the counter-case on this site, and that is why it is quoted at length: same region, same custom, written from inside it.

text.what: Several traditions on this site hold that certain designs may not be worn by people who have not earned them. That rule is theirs to state and not this site's to adjudicate.
text.story:
Cordilleran elders hold that copying an old warrior's chest design marks a person as a killer and brings bad luck, blindness or an early death — and men who fought in the 1960s and 70s declined the marks on that advice. Kalinga inheritance rules held that tattooing could only pass down a bloodline. Sak yant carries rules the bearer keeps afterwards. *Moko kauae* is worn by Māori women.

What this site does: state the rule where a tradition states it, name who states it, and print no design as available. What this site does not do: decide who may wear what, or rank the arguments.
